hints: Focus on atomic numbers first, then remember that losing electrons reduces the count and gaining electrons increases it.
Sodium has atomic number 11, so a neutral Na atom has 11 electrons, but $\text{Na}^{+}$ has lost one to leave 10.
Add up the electrons for three nitrogen atoms and then add one more for the 1- charge on $\text{N}_3^-$ to finish the count.
walkthrough:
**Count electrons in the sodium ion**

Sodium has atomic number 11, so a neutral Na atom has 11 protons and 11 electrons. To form $\text{Na}^{+}$ it loses one electron.

Calculation rule:
$$\text{electrons in Na}^{+} = 11 - 1 = 10$$

**Count electrons in neutral nitrogen atoms**

Nitrogen has atomic number 7, so each N atom has 7 electrons. The azide group contains three N atoms joined together.

Calculation rule:
$$\text{electrons in 3N} = 3 \times 7 = 21$$

**Adjust for the charge on azide**

The azide ion is $\text{N}_3^-$, meaning it carries one extra electron compared to neutral $\text{N}_3$. So we add one more electron.

Calculation rule:
$$\text{electrons in N}_3^- = 21 + 1 = 22$$
So we get 10 for sodium ion and 22 for azide ion.

options.A: This gives 20 electrons for azide, which is the count for neutral $\text{N}_3$ without the extra electron. It forgets to add one electron for the 1- charge on $\text{N}_3^-$.
options.B: This is correct. $\text{Na}^{+}$ has 10 electrons (11 minus 1), and $\text{N}_3^-$ has 22 electrons (3 x 7 plus 1 for the negative charge). Well done for handling both the atom count and the charge.
options.C: This gives 12 for sodium, which confuses atomic number with ion charge. Sodium is element 11, and losing an electron gives 10, not 12. It also misses the extra electron on azide.
options.D: Azide is correct at 22, but sodium is wrong at 12. This trap comes from adding one electron instead of subtracting one when forming the positive $\text{Na}^{+}$ ion.
